title: Cap. XII: Likeness in the thing, not the mode — Calvin vs recentiores
pass_a_gloss: He also gibes at our reply, that the likeness of the opposition is seated in the thing, not in the mode of the thing; and he says we defend Socinus's side rather than Calvin's: when yet he himself in truth departs from Calvin, to whom we cling closely. But how does he refute that reply which above we proved both by authority and by reason? He asks, why then do our people draw from here the mode of our justification, namely through the imputation of Christ's righteousness? This, forsooth, is a splendid way of refuting! Who then are those of ours who draw it from here? Calvin? Martyr? Bucer? Bullinger, and so on? Certainly by no means; but more recent men, turning aside from their footsteps in that matter. But, he says, they do not see how much they wound the common cause, who not only allow this supposedly invincible argument to be snatched from themselves, but also, so far as in them lies, snatch it from us that they may favor the adverse cause. And if we inquire why they so luxuriate in this place, we shall certainly find it is done as a favor to Pelagians, Arminians, Socinians, Anabaptists. On the contrary, we see how much they wound the common cause who either do not know how or refuse to argue well, thrust forward arguments of no strength as invincible, and meanwhile overwhelm their brothers with calumnies. This certainly we both see and grieve over.
pass_b_english: He also gibes at our reply—that the opposition's likeness lies in the thing, not in its mode—and says we take Socinus's part rather than Calvin's, when in fact he is the one leaving Calvin, to whom we hold fast. How does he refute the reply we already proved by authority and reason? He asks why our people then draw from this text the mode of justification, namely by imputing Christ's righteousness. A fine refutation! Who among ours draws that from here—Calvin, Martyr, Bucer, Bullinger, and the rest? Not at all; only later writers who leave their path on this point. They do not see, he says, how they wound the common cause when they let this supposedly invincible argument be torn from them—and, so far as they can, tear it from us to favor the other side. If we ask why they luxuriate so in this place, we shall find it is done to favor Pelagians, Arminians, Socinians, and Anabaptists. We see the opposite: they wound the common cause who cannot or will not argue well, push forward weak proofs as invincible, and meanwhile bury their brothers under slander. That we both see and lament.
source_text: Suggillat etiam nostram responsionem, In re sitam esse similitudinem oppositionis, non in rei modo; ac dicit nos Socini potius quam Calvini partes tueri: cum tamen ipse revera discedat a Calvino, cui nos arcte adhaeremus. Quomodo autem illam responsionem, quam supra & autoritate & ratione comprobavimus, refutat? petit, cur ergo nostrates justificationis nostrae modum, nempe per imputationem justitiae Christi hinc eliciunt? Haec est scilicet egregia refutandi ratio! Quinam vero sunt illi nostrates qui id hinc eliciunt? Calvinus? Martyr? Bucerus? Bullingerus &c? Nequaquam certe; sed recentiores, ab eorum vestigiis ea in re deflectentes. At, inquit, non vident quantum communem causam laedant, qui hoc sibi invictum argumentum non solum eripi patiuntur, sed & nobis, ut adversae causae faveant, quantum in eis situm est, eripiunt. Et si cur hunc locum ita luxent, anquiramus; id in gratiam Pelagianorum, Arminianorum, Socinianorum, Anabaptistarum fieri certo comperiemus. Imo vero videmus quantum causam communem laedant, qui bene argumentari, vel nesciunt vel nolunt, argumentaque nullius roboris pro invictis obtrudunt, & interim fratres suos calumniis obruunt. Hoc certe & videmus & dolemus.
